Name: Giota Detsi
Question: Which Greek island would you like to live on if you had the chance, and why?
Answer: This is a tricky question because most of the islands are truly melancholic in the winter. The tourist facilities (hotels, rooms for rent, tavernas, bars, even groceries) are closed from November to April and most of you will find it depressing to walk in deserted streets…at least, I do! So, the party islands such as Paros or Ios are not for me. Are there any islands with life all year round? Yes, there are and from them, I choose Syros Island. Ermoupolis, the “chora” of Syros is the capital of the Cyclades and has an airport, a daily ferry connection with Piraeus, a hospital, civil services, and university departments. It is a safe place (you can leave the keys on the door) and the 20,000 inhabitants make the place live all seasons. Vaporia, the prestigious district of Ermoupolis, residence of the ship-owners of the island. Besides, Syros has its history and culture, this is the "armor" that protects it because it attracts more sophisticated people and not those who just want a holiday home. Ermoupolis was born 200 years ago, when Chian merchants and sailors, persecuted by the Ottomans, ended up in Syros, they resorted to the natural, sheltered harbor under the medieval acropolis of the island and, starting from humble refugee accommodation, within three decades they managed to set up a small but powerful urban, naval and industrial center. When Athens still looked like a small new city grappling with the ambition to become the capital, Hermoupolis was already the largest shipbuilding center in the Mediterranean and there was an opera house where you could hear an Italian troupe playing La Traviata. The interior of the Apollo Theater in Ermoupolis. The emblem of the cultural development of Ermoupolis was constructed in 1862-1864 to designs of the famous Italian architect Pietro Sambo. Its operation began on April 20, 1864, with Verdi's Rigoletto. In recent years, of course, a change has been taking place throughout the Cyclades (tourism is advancing) that if the brakes are not applied, the situation will dissolve. So, Syros is my choice, at least, as long I can afford it… All the images are from Ταξίδι στη Σύρο: Πώς είναι η Ερμούπολη και το νησί το χειμώνα

Name: Giota Detsi
Question: How did ancient Greeks entertain themselves?
Answer: The Greeks (ancient and modern) are extrovert people, they like to share their moments with others. So, although in antiquity life was hard and most of the day was spent at work (don’t forget that most of them were farmers), dinner with friends (a quite common custom) was a good opportunity to relax and get rid of the stress of the day. Don’t think of the fancy symposia of the wealthy people, there were more like two or more friends (men only!) sharing their food, sipping their wine, and chatting about everything. At the same time, the women would stay in separate rooms and…do the same! In the big urban centers like Athens or Corinth, the unofficial dinners could be more lavish, a banquet. It can include philosophical discussions, dancing, and singing by professional artists who may offer more private entertainment too (that would be a symposium). Or they could also play games with kottabos being the most popular. The purpose of this game was to achieve a goal. As a shot, they used wine that was hurled with the mouth or thrown by hand holding a shallow plate. The target was the scale, a platter attached high to a stick, or floating in a basin of water. Representation of a kottavos scene on an ancient Greek vase. The balance is mounted on a long stick, while the player aims while holding a disc. Attribution 2.5 Generic However, the biggest opportunity for common people to have fun was at the religious festivities. They would dress in their best clothes, and attempt ceremonies, parades, possibly theatrical performances or/and athletic games. They would dance, sing, flirt (legally or not). And…when think of religious festivities, don’t think only of the Olympic Games and the Panathenaea, there were a lot of religious festivities of local or Panhellenic importance…. The spectacular procession of the horsemen in Panathenaea on Parthenon’s frieze. The real event must be quite a spectacle. : http://my-favourite-planet.de/english/europe/greece/attica/athens/acropolis/acropolis-photos-01-015.htm What else could they do to have fun? They played! Games like the chalki myia (mole fly), akininda (statuettes), pentelitha (pentovola), and more that the Greeks among you would recognize for sure…

Question: Can you put yourself into the frame of mind of a nineteenth-century immigrant?
Answer: The Greeks are a nation of diaspora, the ones abroad are more than the Greeks in the homeland (it’s rare to find a Greek family without a member living and working outside Greece). In the early nineteenth century, the riskiest among the exhausted from poverty left for other lands, seeking wealth opportunities. Lots of destinations for them; Russia (the common religion and the already established Greek communities made it a popular destination), other parts of the Ottoman Empire, like Valachia (same as above), and France for the few wealthy ones who wanted a broader and better education, Austria, Italy, and Egypt for the merchants, and the first small wave for the USA for the desperate ones. The latter, the riskiest among the riskiest, mostly fishermen, arrived in Florida, on a land where people spoke a different language, and had a different religion and mentality but the sea was still blue…the Florida community thrived and progressed although none of them ever returned home. sponge ship operated out of Tarpon Springs NEW WAVES OF CHANGE I can understand those people. They were free spirits, seeking more adventure and wealth than a way to feed their family as happened with the big wave of migration to the States in the early 20th century. Those men embarked on the one-month voyage to the unknown and hostile land, practically penniless, knowing that they’d probably never return and seeking a way to support themselves and their family back home. How desperate and determined must they be? Anyway, they weren’t the ones I respect the most but the women that followed. Soon enough, the single among them asked for Greek brides. Poor fathers all over Greece found this a great opportunity to send their girls to America; some believed their girls would have a better life and some others were just glad to get rid of them. For sure none of them asked their daughters’ opinions. Can you imagine a ship full of brides? Young, illiterate girls, going to an unknown land, destined to live next to a man they didn’t know? How frightened must they be? I can’t put myself in their mind, really! Greek brides going to America. Only one of them smiles. greek brides going to america

Question: Why is there no evidence of a multiverse theory?
Answer: There is more than one theory (actually, they are hypotheses) about the multiverse. There are so many that the cosmologist Max Tegmark categorized them into four levels and… this is a bad start because this means that none of them is complete. At level 1, the other universes are extensions of our universe, with the same physical constants and the same physical laws. They are areas that are moving away from us so quickly that their light will never be able to reach us, no matter how much time passes. At level 2, we come across a quite different interpretation of the Multiverse, we have independent universes – bubbles that all arose through the same mechanism and have the same or different physical constants.. According to the theory of inflation, space inherently contains energy, which leads to the rapid expansion of space itself and the appearance of particles, i.e. matter and energy. Schematically, we could say that each universe is like a bubble in the same lake. These bubbles are separated from birth and each follows its own evolutionary path. At level 3, we find the parallel universes of the interpretation of the many worlds of Quantum Mechanics. Each quantum possibility corresponds to another universe. (Image: Scientific American) In Quantum mechanics, the position and behavior of a particle are described by a wave function, that is, by a relationship that gives us the probability that the particle is in a certain region. As long as we do not interact with them, the resulting picture is what they behave as waves. Conversely, when we observe them, that is, we interact with them they are treated as simple particles. The most popular and accepted interpretation of this strange phenomenon is the Copenhagen interpretation. According to it, the Universe is inherently probabilistic and, in essence, at the moment of observation the wave function collapses. That is, the position of the particle takes a specific value based on probabilities. Everett's interpretation of the multiverse doesn’t accept the collapse of the wave function. According to it, there is a universe for every possible quantum state. That is, infinite universes are created each time a particle is observed. Finally, at level 4, all universes that can be described mathematically are included. The criticism of the Multiverse hypothesis (but also of theories such as string theory) is that while they are products of mathematical logical reasoning, they seem to be unfalsifiable. That is, they cannot be debunked or proven experimentally. In other words, they don’t fulfill the fundamental law of science… footnotes Max Tegmark's excellent article in Scientific American which I recommend you study: https://space.mit.edu/home/tegmark/PDF/multiverse_sciam.pdf

Question: What is Ampheion in ancient Greece Thebes?
Answer: Ampheion is one of the most intriguing, controversial, and fascinating monuments of Greek antiquity. It is a tumulus associated with the two sons of Zeus, Zethos and Amphion, who walled Cadmeia, while from the name of Zethos' wife, Thebe, the city was renamed Thebes. The two brothers, according to myths, were buried in a common tomb, located in the northern part of Cadmeia, just outside the "Northern Gates", in a tomb, where according to Pausanias ("Boeotika" 17.4) "earth is the soil of the great". image from Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” image credit Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES A lot of ancient authors referred to the monument such as Xenophon in “Ellinika”, 5:48, Plutarch in “On the Demon of Socrates”, 4, and more. It was a well-known and well-respected monument during antiquity (it wasn’t looted or disturbed by any means until the early Christian years) and detailed descriptions of the monument and its position survived to our days. Ok, it’s a monument connected with mythological heroes, why is it intriguing, controversial, and fascinating? Its shape! image credit Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES It is a mastaba-type stepped pyramidoid with three levels (8.8. 4.4. and 2.2m respectively). Isn’t it fascinating? image from Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” A twin tomb on the top step! On top of the stepped pyramid was found a stone-built tomb which hosted two burials, confirming Pausanias’ words “εν κοινώ” (together). The box-shaped (2.20 x 1.15 meters) tomb consisted of large carved limestone slabs. The excavations brought to light other important items: skeleton remains and gold jewelry that escaped the robbers. image credit Bronze Age - MUSEUM OF THEBES OMG! Is it that old? The technique of the jewelry and the fragments of pottery found, date the burial in the Proto-Helladic (before the Mycenaeans) period ~2,500 BCE. That means that a story that old survived from the Mycenaean era until our days through the ancient authors. How much of the story is true (if any) we can’t tell but is certainly intriguing! More information about the monument. The monument was discovered in 1971 by the archaeologist Theodoros Spyropoulos. He also discovered a vast net of underground corridors under the monument but he was forced to close the dig before even photographing them. Until today, the corridors have not been explored thoroughly. However, the short emergency excavation carried out by the 7th Ephorate of Prehistoric and Classical Antiquities in 2007, immediately below the tumulus, discovered three chamber tombs dug into the natural rock of the hill, as well as a shallow carved grave for a woman with a baby in her arms. The tumulus is accessible although in bad condition. According to the ancient tradition, the inhabitants of the nearby Tithorea in Phocis secretly took soil from Amphion when the sun passed through the constellation Taurus (May). Pausanias says ("Boeotika", 17.4): "The sun conducted him in the heavens". The Tithorians, secretly taking soil from Amphio, brought it to the tomb of Antiope, the mother of the Thebans Dioskouri, and thus their country became more fertile, while the fertility of the Theban land decreased. footnotes Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” ������� �������� ������� Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES
